title: AndroidFlux: Evaluating Failure Recovery and Recovery Action Reward Modeling in Mobile-Use Multimodal Agents

paper.title: AndroidFlux: Evaluating Failure Recovery and Recovery Action Reward Modeling in Mobile-Use Multimodal Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract Mobile-use multimodal agents are typically evaluated by task success from a clean initial state, which does not isolate their ability to recover from intermediate errors. Because mobile environments change dynamically, a general mobile-use agent must complete tasks robustly even from unexpected states and in unseen environments. This requires knowing when and where an agent makes errors, and whether it can recover from errors and subsequent states. To evaluate this capability, we introduce AndroidFlux , a failure-recovery benchmark built on AndroidWorld. AndroidFlux restores recorded trajectories to controlled checkpoints before, at, and after the first recoverable error, so that different agents continue from the same device state and history. On these checkpoints, a complementary reward-modeling benchmark evaluates recovery-action preferences using downstream rollout outcomes. We further release an offline reinforcement learning (RL) dataset that improves both error recovery and overall task success. Our evaluations show that recovery performance only partially correlates with clean-start success, and that explicit reasoning helps only models trained with GUI-domain specific RL.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Multimodal agents now operate real mobile devices, completing user tasks by reading screens and performing touch and text actions over long horizons ( Rawles et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Kong et al., 2025 ) . Existing benchmarks evaluate these agents almost entirely by task success from a clean start, and the strongest models are nearing saturation on them. Yet, a clear gap still remains between benchmark scores and in-the-wild performance. Part of the reason is that a single pass or fail per episode hides what happens inside it: the intermediate failures behind the outcome and which actions helped or hurt along the way. Because mobile environments change dynamically, a general mobile-use agent must complete tasks robustly even from unexpected states and in unseen environments. This requires knowing when and where an agent makes errors, and whether it can recover from errors and subsequent states. Recovery matters even more in recent agentic systems, which increasingly optimize inference cost by assigning easier tasks to smaller agents ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Ong et al., 2024 ) . When a smaller agent stalls, these systems often hand over the unfinished task to a stronger model ( Wei et al., 2026 ) , which must then recover from mistakes it did not make, in a context and device state it did not produce. However, observing these behaviors through clean-start rollouts is expensive: failure states arise only by chance, each one costs a full episode to reach, and the score reflects the whole episode rather than the specific steps where recovery succeeds or fails. Although measuring failure recovery is critical for closing the gap to real-world deployment and for building efficient agentic systems, no existing mobile-use benchmark directly evaluates this capability. To address this, we introduce AndroidFlux (Figure 1 ) to evaluate the failure recovery and recovery-action reward modeling capabilities through controlled replay of policy-induced failures in AndroidWorld. We annotate the first error step t t and restore checkpoints at t − n t{-}n (correct prefix), t t (error committed), and t + 1 t{+}1 (after a positive or negative recovery action). Target agents resume from matched device states with histories re-rendered in their own formats, allowing us to examine how policies handle the same failure and how recovery depends on the preceding actions. Across human-verified and larger LLM-verified sets, recovery performance only partially correlates with clean-start success, showing that existing benchmarks alone are insufficient for assessing an agent’s robustness. We find that explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning also does not consistently improve recovery: general reasoning ability alone does not ensure effective action in a disrupted GUI state. On our reward-modeling benchmark, reward models trained on generic GUI preferences stay near chance, while GUI experts’ own action likelihoods rank recovery actions better, and the two are correct on largely different pairs, suggesting they are complementary. Furthermore, we release an offline RL dataset of 8.5k decision contexts that improves both recovery and clean-start success, offering a practical resource for studying failure recovery without expensive online RL training.

sections.heading: Mobile/GUI benchmarks.
sections.text: GUI-agent benchmarks differ mainly in whether the agent acts in a live environment and what state each episode begins from. AndroidControl supplies static UI-control data along demonstrations, scorable at any step but without consequences ( Li et al., 2024 ) . AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, MobileWorld, and OSWorld provide interactive environments with programmatic verifiers, but most episodes start from the home screen and return one terminal outcome ( Rawles et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Kong et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . Concurrent with this work, GUI-RobustEval benchmarks post-error recovery on desktop agents by resuming after a policy-induced error ( Bu et al., 2026 ) . AndroidFlux instead targets mobile agents and spans controlled checkpoints before, at, and after the first error, enabling cross-agent takeover from inherited context. It further evaluates outcome-grounded recovery-action preferences, evaluating not only whether an agent recovers but whether a reward model can identify the action that makes recovery more likely.

sections.heading: Reward modeling.
sections.text: Mobile GUI agents are typically trained against sparse terminal success ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , while process reward models supply denser signal by scoring intermediate decisions ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , and preference-based reward models are conventionally fit under the Bradley–Terry (BT) interface ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . UI-Genie ( Xiao et al., 2025 ) is the closest GUI precedent, training action- and task-level rewards from rule verification and synthetic corruption. Its negatives, however, are perturbations of correct behavior rather than actions a policy took at a state it had actually broken, and the reward model is trained inside a self-improvement loop with a single agent. The sources of errors used for reward modeling have not yet been scaled across policies, and RL with such rewards remains largely unexplored in both online and offline settings.

sections.heading: 4 AndroidFlux: Error Recovery & Recovery Action Reward Modeling Benchmark
sections.text: To measure whether a policy repairs a broken state and whether a reward model can identify the action that repairs it, we introduce AndroidFlux : a failure-recovery benchmark and a recovery-action reward modeling benchmark, both built on the AndroidWorld environment and tasks. Table 1 overviews them against existing GUI agent benchmarks.

sections.heading: 4.1 Error Recovery Benchmark
sections.text: The error recovery benchmark supplies restored resume points drawn from real policy failures. Its human-verified set is fixed at 80 cases from 6 source models, 65 restored by replaying the recorded action prefix and 15 from saved emulator snapshots where exact replay is not reliable. Its LLM-verified set contains 312 replay-based cases over 104 tasks from 21 source models, extending coverage across a wider pool of failure sources.

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Annotation of the First Error
sections.text: The first error is the initial error in the trajectory a model executes toward its goal, and the only one unaffected by a preceding error. For the human-verified set, human experts reviewed the trajectory step by step and labeled the earliest error. For the LLM-verified set, a two-stage detector–verifier framework implemented with Gemini Flash 3.0 ( Google DeepMind, 2025 ) proposes candidate error steps and re-checks each against the resulting UI state, taking the earliest surviving step as the first error. Because a false label relocates the state at which every downstream recovery experiment begins, the framework is tuned toward precision at the expense of recall, reaching 90.8% step-level precision on the annotated set and so identifying policy-induced first errors reliably. Each error is classified to one of three categories—Stagnation, Direction, and Execution. Further details are reported in Appendix C.7 and C.9 .

sections.heading: 4.2 Recovery Action Reward Modeling Benchmark
sections.text: The AndroidFlux recovery-action reward modeling benchmark fixes the resume state and pairs a positive and a negative next action, and a reward model is expected to rank the pair by which action is more likely to lead to recovery. It contains 100 recovery states over 26 AndroidWorld task types: 72 resume from a detected first error and 28 from an error-free step. We generate source trajectories from ten agents, annotate their first errors with the detector–verifier pipeline, and resume five recovery models from the restored states to obtain candidate recovery actions. Each action candidate is replayed and a panel of twelve agents spanning a wide range of recovery ability rolls out from the resulting state. Preference thus follows from consequence rather than rule or judge: at each state we pair the two candidates whose panel success counts differ most, keeping the pair only when the margin is at least two. The resulting 100 pairs share task, state, screenshots, and history other than the recovery action. Further details are in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 4.3 Dataset: Offline RL Training Dataset for Error Recovery
sections.text: The RL dataset contains 8,499 policy-induced contexts built from source trajectories collected before replay filtering, sampled with seed 42 from four slices: t − n t{-}n (2,097), t − 1 t{-}1 and t t (2,080 each), and successful contexts with verified environment success (2,242). Each is annotated with whether its goal is already satisfied, making termination the correct next action. A checkpoint is the last action in the history, so t − 1 t{-}1 prompts the erroneous action and t t prompts a recovery at t + 1 t{+}1 ; no history extends past the first error. Construction and the training details are given in Appendix E.1 for details.

sections.heading: 5 Main Results
sections.text: All experiments run in the containerized AndroidWorld environment released with the benchmark, which we customize for reproducibility and stability. Every evaluation in this paper is split across container shards running on H100, A40, L40S, and RTX 4090 GPUs.

General-purpose VLMs can recover from inherited failures, but domain-specialized GUI agents are generally more robust around the first-error checkpoint. Agentic frameworks strengthen this effect through inference-time state reassessment and replanning. sections.heading: 5.2 Rewinding vs. Injection by Failure Timing
sections.text: An agent’s mistake can be remedied in two ways. Rewinding returns the agent to the state just before the error and lets it attempt the step again; injection leaves the error in place but hands the agent one correct recovery action and lets it continue from there. In our checkpoints, the value of rewinding is the gap between t − 1 t{-}1 and t t , and the value of injection is the gap between t + 1 + t{+}1^{+} and t + 1 − t{+}1^{-} . Which remedy helps more depends on how far into the task the failure occurs.Splitting the 312 episodes by how many steps the agent had taken before the error, rewinding is most valuable for early failures ( + 8.76 +8.76 pp) and loses most of its benefit for late ones ( + 3.41 +3.41 pp), whereas injection is nearly useless early on and becomes the more helpful remedy late ( + 5.86 +5.86 pp; Table 4 , Figure 3 ). The gap between the two grows by 12.22 12.22 pp, with a 95% confidence interval of [ + 4.1 , + 20.8 ] [+4.1,+20.8] . Because every model attempts every episode, results within an episode are correlated, so the interval resamples episodes rather than individual model runs. The direction of the effect is robust: it holds for 17 of the 18 models individually, across all task-difficulty quartiles, across all trajectory-length terciles, and in both halves of a random episode split. The length-tercile check is the important one, since longer tasks also have longer prefixes; the effect appears within each tercile, so it is not simply a proxy for task length. Within these finer slices the gap is always positive (from + 3.29 +3.29 pp to + 21.03 +21.03 pp) but not always individually significant, since each slice is small; we read them as evidence of a consistent direction rather than of significance in every subgroup. Bucket boundaries were fixed in advance rather than searched. Intuitively, an early mistake costs little context, so a second attempt is cheap and effective; a late mistake sits on top of a long history, and what the agent most needs is not another chance to reason but the one action that gets it back on track. sections.heading: 5.3 Recovery-Action Reward Modeling
sections.text: Table 5 compares training-free scorers, which rank actions by the log-probabilities of expert agents, with trained reward models. On UI-Genie, BT outperforms SFT trained on the same 128K samples from 64K pairs ( 0.904 0.904 vs. 0.878 0.878 ) with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) on Qwen3-VL-8B. The hard SFT only checks whether the predicted correct/incorrect token matches the label, so it cannot order two actions that receive the same token. We therefore also compare the log-probability each action assigns to that token (Soft). Even so, SFT still under-performs BT, which suggests that SFT learns absolute correctness well, while relative preference is better learned through the pairwise BT loss. Scale also matters. Scaling the data from 128K to 256K adds 1.1 points on UI-Genie and 3 points on AndroidFlux on UI-Genie RM BT, so AndroidFlux still separates reward models where UI-Genie is close to saturation. Still, both reward models stay near chance on AndroidFlux. This indicates that UI-Genie’s preference data, built by injecting errors into clean trajectories, does not provide enough signal to learn recovery. The GUI experts, in contrast, already hold these preferences. Without any reward-model training, their likelihoods reach 0.71 0.71 – 0.74 0.74 on UI-Genie and 0.58 0.58 – 0.60 0.60 on AndroidFlux. Their advantage over BT-256K comes almost entirely from error-path pairs, where each expert ranks 6–8 more of the 72 pairs correctly. Finally, these sources are complementary. The best single scorer ranks 60 of the 100 pairs correctly, but at least one of the five agents ranks 82 correctly, and adding BT-256K raises this to 87, because agent likelihoods and the UI-Genie reward model fail on different pairs. Combining the agents’ preferences with the more general preferences of a UI-Genie reward model could cover most of the preferences in AndroidFlux. Further details are in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 5.4 Offline Reinforcement Learning
sections.text: We further examine whether training on the AndroidFlux offline RL dataset improves error recovery and clean-start success. Building on prior work that optimizes VLM and LLM based agents with offline RL ( Qian et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) and online RL ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , we finetune Qwen3-VL-4B with LoRA using offline GRPO with Group Preference Reward Shaping (GPRS) ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , without executing sampled actions in the environment during training. We use UI-Genie BT-128K as the reward model and fix the training budget at 2.4K samples. We compare UI-Genie reward modeling data with AndroidFlux offline RL data collected at the first-error checkpoint t t , t − 1 t{-}1 , and mixtures of these sources. Rewards rise similarly across mixtures despite different downstream success. Table 6 shows that the source of offline training contexts substantially affects downstream behavior. Training on the UI-Genie reward modeling dataset alone provides little overall benefit and reduces recovery from first-error states. In contrast, every run with our curated offline RL dataset outperforms the UI-Genie 100% run in mean success. Training exclusively at the first-error checkpoint produces the strongest recovery but degrades clean-start performance, indicating that concentrating only on failure states can over-specialize the policy. Combining the conventional reward modeling dataset with our policy-induced, failure-centered contexts largely removes this trade-off. In particular, the UI 40% / t t 35% / t − 1 t{-}1 25% mixture improves both clean-start execution and error recovery over the UI-Genie 100% run, while also outperforming the base policy under both evaluation conditions. Moreover, most mixtures improve clean performance despite using fewer UI-Genie samples, suggesting that states surrounding first errors provide useful supervision beyond recovery itself. These results suggest that our offline RL dataset provides a more persistent learning signal in both clean runs and failure recovery. Despite the performance differences on both the UI-Genie and AndroidFlux reward modeling evaluation sets, Figure 4 indicates that optimization remains stable across all data mixtures. The mean GPRS reward rises similarly in every run, but it is not a direct measure of policy quality, since the statistic is inflated by duplicate sampled actions within each group. Indeed, the UI-Genie 100% run reaches a comparable final GPRS reward despite the weakest downstream performance. The underlying reward-model scores show a clearer difference: UI-Genie-only training plateaus and then declines later in training, whereas most runs with diverse contexts around the error step keep improving through the final training window, ending with a larger net gain. Overall, these results indicate that our policy-induced failure contexts provide an informative training signal in offline RL for generalized GUI agents without computationally heavy online environments.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations and Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced AndroidFlux, a benchmark that evaluates mobile-use agents on recovering from policy-induced first errors and reward models on ranking recovery actions. However, it covers only AndroidWorld and first recoverable errors that can be reconstructed by replay or snapshots, so chains of interacting errors and other GUI environments remain open. The LLM-verified set also inherits noise and source-model imbalance from the detector–verifier pipeline, and recovery success remains sensitive to Android nondeterminism. Even so, our results show that recovering from a committed error is a capability distinct from clean-start success, with domain-specific RL and agentic frameworks far more robust than general-purpose or imitation-trained models. Our reward modeling benchmark demonstrates that reward models trained on conventional GUI preferences stay near chance on recovery states, while the likelihoods of GUI expert agents rank recovery actions more accurately. Furthermore, we find that our curated offline RL dataset improves both clean-start and recovery success under a fixed training budget, showing that policy-induced failure states are effective training signal. Together, our contributions and findings establish failure recovery and recovery-aware reward modeling as key evaluation targets for building robust GUI agents. Appendix

sections.text: Six source models each attempted 112 AndroidWorld tasks, yielding 672 trajectories in total. The 112 tasks were obtained by excluding four of the original 116 tasks due to environment issues that prevented reliable execution or evaluation. All 672 trajectories were then manually reviewed step by step. sections.heading: C.6.1 Replay and Snapshot
sections.text: The 80 human-verified cases are divided into 65 replay-based and 15 snapshot-based cases according to whether the annotated error state can be reproduced by action replay. For the 65 replay-based cases, we re-execute in the emulator the source model’s recorded action sequence through the annotated first-error step t t . A case is considered replayable when this procedure reaches the same erroneous state observed in the original trajectory. Once that state is reached, the recovering policy takes over and continues the task from the restored state. Its inherited history is constructed from the source trajectory metadata and rendered in the target policy’s native format, as detailed in Appendix C.8 . For the remaining 15 cases, replaying the recorded actions from the task’s initial state does not reproduce the original error state. A primary source of such mismatch is residual environment state from preceding tasks. For example, when the original AndroidWorld tasks are executed sequentially, previously used applications may change their positions in recency-ordered interfaces; replaying an individual task in isolation does not reproduce this preceding interaction history and can therefore lead to a different state despite executing the same actions. For these cases, we manually reconstruct the emulator to match the original error state and save it as a VM snapshot, allowing evaluation to resume directly from that state. The inherited history remains based on the original source trajectory, with only the minimal state-dependent details responsible for the replay mismatch adjusted to remain consistent with the reconstructed state. The recovering policy then receives this reconstructed state and history under the same evaluation protocol as in the replay-based cases.

( 3 ) in the live emulator at k = t k=t , the checkpoint at which the error has been committed under an otherwise correct prefix. The environment is first restored to s ^ t \hat{s}_{t} by re-executing the recorded action prefix a 0 : t a_{0:t} under the same task seed; for the 15 15 human-verified trajectories whose replay does not reach the error state (Appendix C.6.1 ), the manually reconstructed emulator VM snapshot is loaded instead. The target policy π \pi then receives the reconstructed context h t π h^{\pi}_{t} , built by re-rendering the schema-neutral step records of Appendix C.8 into π \pi ’s native prompt format, together with the live observation of the restored screen. Nothing in that context marks the prefix as replayed, erroneous, or authored by another model: from the target’s perspective the episode is simply in progress, and steps 0 0 through t t read as its own past actions. The target is therefore never told that a recovery is required—noticing the broken state is part of what AndroidFlux measures. From step t + 1 t+1 the target acts autonomously over the action space of Table 7 , and actions are executed on the device exactly as in a clean-start rollout. The episode terminates when the target emits a terminal action ( status or answer ) or exhausts the remaining step budget H − t H-t , and the terminal state is scored by the task’s programmatic verifier r r . A trajectory is thus credited only when the target both repairs the effect of a t a_{t} and completes the remainder of the task; partial repair without completion is scored as failure. When π = π src \pi=\pi_{\mathrm{src}} the run measures self-recovery, and otherwise the target inherits a failure and a history authored by a different model—the cross-agent condition of Table 16 . Because the restored state and the rendered prefix are both fixed before any target is run, the same broken state is handed identically to every agent in the roster, so differences in success rate are attributable to the recovering policy alone. sections.text: The unit is a (model, episode) pair, and the outcome of a run is 1 if it succeeds and 0 otherwise. sections.heading: C.7 First Error and Recovery Across Error Categories
sections.text: We categorize first errors by behavior rather than by widget or app type. Each step is viewed as a triple of (intended goal direction, chosen action, observed screen transition), and the three classes are distinguished by which element of this triple is broken. Classes are checked in a fixed priority order — stagnation → \rightarrow direction → \rightarrow execution — so that a repeated action is labeled as stagnation without further inspecting its direction or realization. Figure 5 shows, for each class, the screen immediately before and after a representative first-error step (a: stagnation, b: direction, c: execution), and Tables 21 and 22 summarize the per-category counts for the two verified sets.

sections.heading: Stagnation.
sections.text: The agent re-issues an action that has already failed on an essentially unchanged screen, or oscillates between states, so that the trajectory makes no visible progress (Fig. 5(a) ). The failure lies not in what the agent intends but in the fact that it repeats the attempt without adapting. A first unsuccessful attempt is not counted: the error step is the point at which repetition is established (typically the second or later identical attempt), and actions with intrinsically subtle visual effects (e.g., text editing, keyboard input) are excluded from the “no screen change” criterion. Observed sub-patterns include identical re-taps on the same element, repeated scrolling over an unchanged list, re-entering an already-failed route, and acting on a nonexistent or already-achieved UI state.

sections.heading: Direction.
sections.text: The action executes successfully, but it moves the trajectory away from the goal (Fig. 5(b) ): the agent commits to a visibly wrong target, screen, date, or app, regresses by dismissing progress it has already achieved, abandons a route on which the required affordance is already exposed, or ignores a visible contradiction. Local execution is correct; the choice is not. Exploratory route-opening, reversible entries into a wrong menu, and app switches for source verification are protected as valid — a direction error is assigned only when a wrong target or state is committed, or when the agent leaves a required screen without justification. This class subsumes goal-regressive, goal-irrelevant, goal-direction, and unhandled system-error behaviors in our finer-grained taxonomy.

sections.heading: Execution.
sections.text: The agent targets the right element with the right kind of action, but the action’s local effect is wrong or absent (Fig. 5(c) ): the committed text, value, or selection differs from the intent, the tap lands on a neighboring control, or a launch/save/toggle produces no state change. The plan is correct; the realization is not. The judgment unit is strictly the current step’s intent versus its immediate outcome — an error is assigned when the immediately following screenshot shows an incorrect committed value, but not merely because the overall task remains unfinished, and stale UI or a missing toast after a correctly targeted commit is not presumed to be a failure.

sections.heading: Boundary between stagnation and execution.
sections.text: “No screen change” appears in both classes; the distinction is repetition. The first task-critical action that produces no effect (e.g., an app launch or toggle that fails) is an execution error, whereas re-attempting an action that has already failed is stagnation. Human-verified labels follow this convention consistently.

sections.heading: Canonical record fields.
sections.text: Agents differ in what they emit alongside the action and in how they render history: window length, whether reasoning is retained, and summary format all vary with Φ π \Phi_{\pi} . Replaying a trajectory under a different policy therefore requires a canonical intermediate. Each recorded response is inverted to the schema-neutral record of Table 23 , then re-rendered in the target agent’s native format, so no agent receives another agent’s prompt format verbatim. Fields the source agent does not emit are synthesized, so every evaluated agent receives a complete history in the form it expects. The accessibility tree is deliberately not stored: agents that consume it receive the live tree from the restored state at resume time, since a recorded tree would describe the source trajectory’s screen rather than the one the target is looking at. Each episode wraps these steps with the task, source model, coordinate convention, replay stop k k , and annotated first error t t . Normalizing to a shared action schema decouples the record from the source model’s coordinate convention, so each adapter re-emits the units its target expects. A record stores the full prefix and defers truncation to the adapter, which slices the latest steps under the target’s own history length. One file holds a prebuilt variant per replay stop, so the t − 1 t{-}1 / t t / t + 1 t{+}1 conditions are materialized ahead of time rather than recomputed per run.

sections.heading: Synthesizing the absent fields.
sections.text: summary is what a recovering agent is most exposed to, so it is synthesized under a two-tier rule preferring authenticity but enforcing neutrality. We reuse the source model’s own summary only if it is plain prose, opens with a past-tense verb, and survives sanitization: pronouns and role prefixes are stripped and purpose clauses truncated, since a stated purpose is the source model’s belief about its own plan and would import that plan into another policy’s context. Any candidate mentioning error, mistake, replay or recovery is discarded—a transcript narrating its own failure would tell the target that something has gone wrong, precisely the inference the benchmark measures. Otherwise we synthesize from an action-type template, of which thought is the imperative form. The filters are strict and most steps fall through, which is the conservative outcome: the history reads uniformly across source models, stating what was done without why or that it was wrong.

Because context is fixed before replay, a run falling back to an emulator snapshot receives an identical history, so the three conditions differ only in where the prefix stops. sections.heading: C.9 Detector–Verifier First Error Detection Framework
sections.text: Human annotation does not scale to a source-model pool of this size, so the LLM-verified set is labeled by a two-stage pipeline, both stages implemented with Gemini Flash 3.0. A detector reads a sliding window of ten step screenshots with the executed actions and proposes clustered error candidates; a verifier then re-checks each candidate against the resulting UI state and returns a single first-error step. We tuned both stages toward precision at the expense of recall, since a missed error only reduces coverage whereas a false label changes the state at which every downstream experiment begins. Table 24 reports the outcome. Aggregated over six source models, the verifier raises step-level precision from 87.2 to 90.8 while leaving recall essentially unchanged, confirming that it removes false candidates rather than trading one error type for another. The per-source breakdown shows the operating point holding across the pool: step-level precision stays between 80.0 and 94.9 on every source model, whereas recall varies far more widely, from 37.8 on Mobile-Agent-v3-32B to 70.1 on Qwen3-VL-2B. Recall tracks how legible a model’s failures are—weaker policies produce blunter, more detectable errors—but because coverage loss is the tolerated failure mode, this variation costs breadth rather than correctness. The one row that stands apart is Gemini Flash, whose high step-level precision (94.9) coincides with the lowest trajectory-level accuracy (55.0), indicating that its errors are correctly identified when found but more often missed at the trajectory level. sections.heading: Appendix D AndroidFlux: Recovery Action Reward Modeling Benchmark
sections.text: The recovery-action reward modeling benchmark asks whether a reward model can rank two actions proposed at the same AndroidWorld checkpoint by their downstream recoverability, with the preference grounded in environment outcomes rather than local heuristics or an LLM judge. Construction proceeds in five stages: source trajectories are generated and their first errors annotated, checkpoints are restored from them, candidate recovery actions are collected into a group at each checkpoint, a fixed panel rolls out from every executed candidate, and the resulting outcome margin determines the released pair.

sections.heading: Pair selection and outcome margin.
sections.text: Selection runs independently within each group, taking the highest-scoring candidate as the positive action a g + a^{+}_{g} and the lowest-scoring as the negative a g − a^{-}_{g} . The two canonicalized actions must differ, so the same action proposed by two models cannot receive opposite labels. When several candidates occupy one success tier we favor the generator used least often in that role so far, which improves source coverage without overriding the panel outcome; both sides of a pair therefore share the task, checkpoint state, screenshot, and history, differing only in the recovery action. A pair’s raw margin is Δ g = S g ​ ( a g + ) − S g ​ ( a g − ) \Delta_{g}=S_{g}(a^{+}_{g})-S_{g}(a^{-}_{g}) , and only groups with Δ g ≥ 2 \Delta_{g}\geq 2 are released, so every pair is separated by panel success count alone. Groups below that threshold are dropped rather than resolved by a secondary signal: success counts saturate when most of the panel recovers from every candidate, and we prefer to discard those groups than to rest a preference on recovery efficiency. The released set therefore contains no tie-broken pair, and its 100 targets are all non-degenerate.

sections.heading: UI Genie RM
sections.text: We train three reward models with the UI Genie preference data from the same Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct checkpoint: two BT models that learn a scalar reward with a pairwise preference loss, one on 64K and one on 128K pairs, and a generative SFT model that predicts a single correct/incorrect classification token with next-token cross-entropy. Training data for all three comes from the initial, UI-Genie-RM-517k release, using the context variant that retains the last five interaction steps; each example therefore carries at most five past screenshots, so that sequence length and image budget stay bounded and identical across objectives. From this corpus we draw 64K and 128K chosen–rejected pairs, spanning 82,960 and 95,498 unique referenced images, after removing every pair that overlaps the UI Genie evaluation set; the 128K set contains the 64K set. BT consumes these pairs directly and is trained to assign the higher scalar reward to the chosen action; SFT expands each of the 64K pairs into its two sides, giving 128K pointwise rows labeled with a correct/incorrect token. Gradient accumulation is doubled for SFT so that SFT and the 64K BT model observe the same 64 pairs per optimizer step, holding the visual contexts and actions fixed across objectives. The 128K BT model keeps every other setting and trains for twice as many steps, so the two BT models differ only in data scale. Table 28 reports the complete training configuration. sections.heading: E.1 AndroidFlux Offline RL Dataset for error recovery
sections.text: The reinforcement learning corpus supplies the decision points a policy is optimized on, drawn from the same replayed AndroidFlux trajectories as the benchmarks. Each prompt restores a device state together with the history that led to it and the goal still to be satisfied. Construction proceeds in three stages: checkpoints are restored at four positions around the first annotated error, prompts whose goal disagrees with their source trajectory are removed, and every remaining prompt is annotated with whether its state already completes the task. Training sets are then sampled from the resulting corpus.

sections.heading: Dataset Generation.
sections.text: Source trajectories come from ten agents executing AndroidWorld tasks: Qwen3-VL-2B, -4B, -8B and -32B, GUI-Owl-7B, GUI-Owl-1.5-2B, -8B and -32B, Mobile-Agent-v3-7B, and MAI-UI-8B. As in the reward-modeling benchmark, task instances are produced by the AndroidWorld task generation pipeline, which instantiates each task template with randomly sampled parameters. The corpus covers 90 AndroidWorld root tasks. Trajectories in which the detector–verifier pipeline (Appendix C.9 ) locates a first error supply the t t , t − 1 t{-}1 and t − n t{-}n prompts, and trajectories that the AndroidWorld verifier marks successful supply the successful prompts. A prompt pairs the task goal with the executed history up to its checkpoint and the screen produced by the last action. Each history step is rendered as one natural-language line—the source agent’s own action or summary text where it provides one, otherwise a deterministic narration of the canonical action (Appendix C.8 )—so prompts from different source agents share a single format. The checkpoint is the last action in the history, so a t − 1 t{-}1 prompt asks for the erroneous action, a t t prompt asks for the action at t + 1 t{+}1 , and no history extends past the first error. Finally, each prompt’s goal is compared with the goal recorded at the first step of its source trajectory.

sections.heading: Checkpoint positions.
sections.text: Prompts are taken at four positions relative to the first annotated error t t : at t t , with the error already committed; at t − 1 t{-}1 , one step before it, while the mistake is still avoidable; at t − n t{-}n , from a correct prefix well before it; and from trajectories that reached the goal ( successful ), which supply healthy decisions to balance the error-derived positions. All twenty unseen-test task types are excluded. Table 29 29(a) gives the distribution; each position contributes close to a quarter of the corpus.

sections.text: Every prompt is annotated with is_next_terminate , which marks states that already satisfy the goal, so that the correct next action is terminate . A positive label is assigned only when completion is established from the restored state; a negative label means only that it was not. sections.heading: Policy.
sections.text: All offline-RL experiments initialize from Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (revision ebb281ec ). We finetune the language-model component using LoRA with rank r = 64 r{=}64 and scaling factor α = 32 \alpha{=}32 , applied to all linear layers. The vision tower and vision–language aligner remain frozen. For each training context, the policy input consists of the system prompt containing the tool schema, the task goal, the latest 10 history steps rendered as natural-language text, and the current screenshot. The policy outputs a short reasoning and action description followed by a single tool call, with spatial coordinates represented on a normalized 0 0 – 1000 1000 grid.

sections.heading: GRPO optimization.
sections.text: We use the GRPO implementation in ms-swift . For every prompt, the policy samples K = 8 K{=}8 candidate completions. Each optimization step contains 16 prompts and therefore 128 sampled completions. All runs contain exactly 2,400 prompts and are trained for 150 steps, corresponding to one epoch over the prompt set. We use a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} , 5% warmup, and cosine decay to 0.1 0.1 times the initial learning rate. The KL coefficient is β = 10 − 3 \beta=10^{-3} . Rollouts use temperature 0.9 0.9 , top- p p 0.95 0.95 , and a maximum completion length of 512 tokens.

sections.heading: Reward model.
sections.text: Rewards come from the frozen UI-Genie Bradley–Terry reward model trained on 128K balanced UI-Genie pairs (BT-128K in Table 5 ). Its input is the task goal, the full executed history as text, up to the five most recent screenshots, and the full policy completion (reasoning, action description and tool call) as the candidate. Candidate coordinates are rescaled from the policy’s 0 0 – 1000 1000 grid to the pixel resolution declared in the reward model’s system prompt, which is the space the reward model was trained on.

sections.heading: Group Preference Reward Shaping.
sections.text: Let r i r_{i} denote the scalar reward-model score assigned to candidate i i in a group of K = 8 K=8 samples. Following GPRS ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , we define the group win share B i = 1 K ∑ j = 1 K 𝟙 [ r i ≥ r j ] , B_{i}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbb{1}[r_{i}\geq r_{j}], (4) and use the centered value A i = B i − 1 K ​ ∑ m = 1 K B m A_{i}=B_{i}-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{m=1}^{K}B_{m} (5) as the advantage. We do not divide by the within-group standard deviation. An unparseable completion receives B i = 0 B_{i}=0 , but remains in the group and therefore still acts as an opponent when computing the win shares of parseable candidates.

sections.heading: Terminate guard.
sections.text: Reward-model ranking alone can otherwise assign positive reward to a syntactically valid terminate action even when the current task has not yet been completed. We therefore apply a termination guard after reward scoring. For a candidate whose parsed action type is terminate , we set B i = 0 B_{i}=0 unless the current AndroidFlux context is labelled is_next_terminate=True , indicating that the goal has already been satisfied and termination is the appropriate next action. UI-Genie contexts do not contain this annotation; for these rows, we fall back to whether the reference action is a terminating action. The guard changes only the shaped policy reward and does not modify the underlying reward-model score.

sections.heading: Terminal-state annotation.
sections.text: Every released AndroidFlux RL context contains an is_next_terminate annotation specifying whether the task goal is already satisfied at that state, such that the correct next action is termination. The labels are produced with Gemini-3.8-Flash using two agreeing passes, a strict acceptance gate, and consistency checks across neighbouring trajectory states. These annotations are used by the termination guard during policy optimization.

sections.heading: UI-Genie pool.
sections.text: For generic GUI training states, we deduplicate the 64K balanced UI-Genie reward-model pairs into 42,304 prompts and draw a 12,000-prompt pool stratified by history length, reference action type and app domain (seed 42).

sections.heading: Training-mixture construction.
sections.text: All offline RL experiments use the same budget of 2,400 training prompts, while varying only the source distribution. We construct six training sets from generic UI-Genie contexts and AndroidFlux contexts at the first-error checkpoint t t and one step before the error t − 1 t{-}1 . Each source pool is shuffled once (seed 42) and every set takes the first k k prompts of each pool, so the sets are nested; the t t -only set cycles the 2,080 available t t prompts and repeats 320 of them. No reward-model or rollout-based filtering is applied. The resulting training sets are summarized below. sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate checkpoint 150 on the 65 replay-based, human-verified AndroidWorld tasks, with one episode per task and condition and greedy decoding. In the clean condition, each task begins from its original initial state. In error t t , we replay the recorded source trajectory to the state containing the effect of its first error and ask the learned policy to recover and complete the task. Success is determined by the AndroidWorld programmatic task checker.

sections.heading: Variance and scope of the mixture study.
sections.text: Each training distribution is run with a single seed and evaluated on 65 tasks per condition. As a reference for run-to-run variability, two UI-only runs from an earlier training recipe that differed only in random seed differed by 2/65 tasks (3.1 points) on clean evaluation and 4/65 tasks (6.1 points) on error- t t evaluation. We therefore interpret the main experiment through the consistent improvement of AndroidFlux-containing mixtures over UI-only, rather than treating individual pairwise differences as independently significant. The four mixtures form a small grid intended to test whether generic and failure-centered states are complementary; they should not be interpreted as an optimized mixture ratio.

Because mobile environments change dynamically, a general mobile-use agent must complete tasks robustly even from unexpected states and in unseen environments. This requires knowing when and where an agent makes errors, and whether it can recover from errors and subsequent states. To evaluate this capability, we introduce AndroidFlux , a failure-recovery benchmark built on AndroidWorld. AndroidFlux restores recorded trajectories to controlled checkpoints before, at, and after the first recoverable error, so that different agents continue from the same device state and history. On these checkpoints, a complementary reward-modeling benchmark evaluates recovery-action preferences using downstream rollout outcomes. We further release an offline reinforcement learning (RL) dataset that improves both error recovery and overall task success. Our evaluations show that recovery performance only partially correlates with clean-start success, and that explicit reasoning helps only models trained with GUI-domain specific RL. Full trans. marks whether all three phases around the first error are covered; t + 1 t{+}1 rec. action gives which recovery actions are supplied at the post-error state; RM eval marks whether the benchmark offers action preference evaluation for reward models. 1 Introduction Multimodal agents now operate real mobile devices, completing user tasks by reading screens and performing touch and text actions over long horizons ( Rawles et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Kong et al., 2025 ) . Existing benchmarks evaluate these agents almost entirely by task success from a clean start, and the strongest models are nearing saturation on them. Yet, a clear gap still remains between benchmark scores and in-the-wild performance. Part of the reason is that a single pass or fail per episode hides what happens inside it: the intermediate failures behind the outcome and which actions helped or hurt along the way. Because mobile environments change dynamically, a general mobile-use agent must complete tasks robustly even from unexpected states and in unseen environments. This requires knowing when and where an agent makes errors, and whether it can recover from errors and subsequent states. Recovery matters even more in recent agentic systems, which increasingly optimize inference cost by assigning easier tasks to smaller agents ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Ong et al., 2024 ) . When a smaller agent stalls, these systems often hand over the unfinished task to a stronger model ( Wei et al., 2026 ) , which must then recover from mistakes it did not make, in a context and device state it did not produce. However, observing these behaviors through clean-start rollouts is expensive: failure states arise only by chance, each one costs a full episode to reach, and the score reflects the whole episode rather than the specific steps where recovery succeeds or fails. Although measuring failure recovery is critical for closing the gap to real-world deployment and for building efficient agentic systems, no existing mobile-use benchmark directly evaluates this capability. To address this, we introduce AndroidFlux (Figure 1 ) to evaluate the failure recovery and recovery-action reward modeling capabilities through controlled replay of policy-induced failures in AndroidWorld. We annotate the first error step t t and restore checkpoints at t − n t{-}n (correct prefix), t t (error committed), and t + 1 t{+}1 (after a positive or negative recovery action). Target agents resume from matched device states with histories re-rendered in their own formats, allowing us to examine how policies handle the same failure and how recovery depends on the preceding actions. Across human-verified and larger LLM-verified sets, recovery performance only partially correlates with clean-start success, showing that existing benchmarks alone are insufficient for assessing an agent’s robustness. We find that explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning also does not consistently improve recovery: general reasoning ability alone does not ensure effective action in a disrupted GUI state. On our reward-modeling benchmark, reward models trained on generic GUI preferences stay near chance, while GUI experts’ own action likelihoods rank recovery actions better, and the two are correct on largely different pairs, suggesting they are complementary. Furthermore, we release an offline RL dataset of 8.5k decision contexts that improves both recovery and clean-start success, offering a practical resource for studying failure recovery without expensive online RL training. 2 Related Work Mobile/GUI benchmarks. GUI-agent benchmarks differ mainly in whether the agent acts in a live environment and what state each episode begins from. AndroidControl supplies static UI-control data along demonstrations, scorable at any step but without consequences ( Li et al., 2024 ) . AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, MobileWorld, and OSWorld provide interactive environments with programmatic verifiers, but most episodes start from the home screen and return one terminal outcome ( Rawles et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Kong et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . Concurrent with this work, GUI-RobustEval benchmarks post-error recovery on desktop agents by resuming after a policy-induced error ( Bu et al., 2026 ) . AndroidFlux instead targets mobile agents and spans controlled checkpoints before, at, and after the first error, enabling cross-agent takeover from inherited context. It further evaluates outcome-grounded recovery-action preferences, evaluating not only whether an agent recovers but whether a reward model can identify the action that makes recovery more likely. Reward modeling. Mobile GUI agents are typically trained against sparse terminal success ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , while process reward models supply denser signal by scoring intermediate decisions ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) , and preference-based reward models are conventionally fit under the Bradley–Terry (BT) interface ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . UI-Genie ( Xiao et al., 2025 ) is the closest GUI precedent, training action- and task-level rewards from rule verification and synthetic corruption. Its negatives, however, are perturbations of correct behavior rather than actions a policy took at a state it had actually broken, and the reward model is trained inside a self-improvement loop with a single agent. The sources of errors used for reward modeling have not yet been scaled across policies, and RL with such rewards remains largely unexplored in both online and offline settings. 3 Problem Formulation Preliminaries. Both actions in a pair share the task, state, and history. 4 AndroidFlux: Error Recovery & Recovery Action Reward Modeling Benchmark To measure whether a policy repairs a broken state and whether a reward model can identify the action that repairs it, we introduce AndroidFlux : a failure-recovery benchmark and a recovery-action reward modeling benchmark, both built on the AndroidWorld environment and tasks. Table 1 overviews them against existing GUI agent benchmarks. 4.1 Error Recovery Benchmark The error recovery benchmark supplies restored resume points drawn from real policy failures. Its human-verified set is fixed at 80 cases from 6 source models, 65 restored by replaying the recorded action prefix and 15 from saved emulator snapshots where exact replay is not reliable. Its LLM-verified set contains 312 replay-based cases over 104 tasks from 21 source models, extending coverage across a wider pool of failure sources. 4.1.1 Annotation of the First Error The first error is the initial error in the trajectory a model executes toward its goal, and the only one unaffected by a preceding error. For the human-verified set, human experts reviewed the trajectory step by step and labeled the earliest error. For the LLM-verified set, a two-stage detector–verifier framework implemented with Gemini Flash 3.0 ( Google DeepMind, 2025 ) proposes candidate error steps and re-checks each against the resulting UI state, taking the earliest surviving step as the first error. Because a false label relocates the state at which every downstream recovery experiment begins, the framework is tuned toward precision at the expense of recall, reaching 90.8% step-level precision on the annotated set and so identifying policy-induced first errors reliably. Each error is classified to one of three categories—Stagnation, Direction, and Execution. Further details are reported in Appendix C.7 and C.9 . 4.2 Recovery Action Reward Modeling Benchmark The AndroidFlux recovery-action reward modeling benchmark fixes the resume state and pairs a positive and a negative next action, and a reward model is expected to rank the pair by which action is more likely to lead to recovery. It contains 100 recovery states over 26 AndroidWorld task types: 72 resume from a detected first error and 28 from an error-free step. We generate source trajectories from ten agents, annotate their first errors with the detector–verifier pipeline, and resume five recovery models from the restored states to obtain candidate recovery actions. Each action candidate is replayed and a panel of twelve agents spanning a wide range of recovery ability rolls out from the resulting state. Preference thus follows from consequence rather than rule or judge: at each state we pair the two candidates whose panel success counts differ most, keeping the pair only when the margin is at least two. The resulting 100 pairs share task, state, screenshots, and history other than the recovery action. Further details are in Appendix D . 4.3 Dataset: Offline RL Training Dataset for Error Recovery The RL dataset contains 8,499 policy-induced contexts built from source trajectories collected before replay filtering, sampled with seed 42 from four slices: t − n t{-}n (2,097), t − 1 t{-}1 and t t (2,080 each), and successful contexts with verified environment success (2,242). Each is annotated with whether its goal is already satisfied, making termination the correct next action. A checkpoint is the last action in the history, so t − 1 t{-}1 prompts the erroneous action and t t prompts a recovery at t + 1 t{+}1 ; no history extends past the first error. Construction and the training details are given in Appendix E.1 for details. 5 Main Results All experiments run in the containerized AndroidWorld environment released with the benchmark, which we customize for reproducibility and stability. Every evaluation in this paper is split across container shards running on H100, A40, L40S, and RTX 4090 GPUs. 5.1 Failure Recovery Across Agent Architectures Table 2 shows a clear progression in recovery capability across agent architectures. General-purpose VLMs can recover from inherited failures, but domain-specialized GUI agents are generally more robust around the first-error checkpoint. On the human-verified set, GUI-Owl-1.5-8B achieves 40.0 40.0 at t all t_{\text{all}} , compared with 28.8 28.8 , 30.0 30.0 , and 27.5 27.5 for Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-32B, and Gemini Flash 3.0. The same pattern holds from t − 1 t{-}1 to t t : most models are affected by the committed error, but stronger expert policies retain more of their pre-error performance. This suggests that training for interactive GUI control provides robustness to off-distribution states beyond clean-start capability. Agentic frameworks strengthen this effect through inference-time state reassessment and replanning. Mobile-Agent-v3-7B reaches 35.4 35.4 at t rep t_{\mathrm{rep}} , compared with 24.6 24.6 for GUI-Owl-7B, with the gap widening on the LLM-verified set. MobileRun provides the strongest example: using Gemini Flash 3.0 within the framework raises recovery from 27.5 27.5 to 67.5 67.5 at t all t_{\text{all}} on the human-verified set and from 39.7 39.7 to 67.0 67.0 at t t on the LLM-verified set. It also remains strong after either injected recovery action. These results show that recovery depends not only on the underlying model, but also on inference-time scaling mechanisms for reflection, correction, and replanning. Table 3 and Figure 2 compare matched instruct and explicit CoT reasoning variants within each model family, with Gemini Flash 3.0 providing a same-model thinking on/off control. Explicit CoT does not uniformly improve recovery: Qwen3-VL-32B and Gemini Flash 3.0 perform worse at t t with reasoning enabled, whereas GUI-Owl-1.5-32B and GPT-5.6 Terra improve substantially. This suggests that reasoning acquired through general-domain RL does not necessarily transfer to interactive GUI recovery. In contrast, GUI-Owl and GPT-5.6 Terra apply reasoning-oriented RL in the target GUI domain, and their reasoning variants consistently improve recovery, indicating that domain-aligned RL enhances error recovery performance. Rewinding returns the agent to the state just before the error and lets it attempt the step again; injection leaves the error in place but hands the agent one correct recovery action and lets it continue from there. In our checkpoints, the value of rewinding is the gap between t − 1 t{-}1 and t t , and the value of injection is the gap between t + 1 + t{+}1^{+} and t + 1 − t{+}1^{-} . Which remedy helps more depends on how far into the task the failure occurs.Splitting the 312 episodes by how many steps the agent had taken before the error, rewinding is most valuable for early failures ( + 8.76 +8.76 pp) and loses most of its benefit for late ones ( + 3.41 +3.41 pp), whereas injection is nearly useless early on and becomes the more helpful remedy late ( + 5.86 +5.86 pp; Table 4 , Figure 3 ). Because every model attempts every episode, results within an episode are correlated, so the interval resamples episodes rather than individual model runs. The direction of the effect is robust: it holds for 17 of the 18 models individually, across all task-difficulty quartiles, across all trajectory-length terciles, and in both halves of a random episode split. The length-tercile check is the important one, since longer tasks also have longer prefixes; the effect appears within each tercile, so it is not simply a proxy for task length. Within these finer slices the gap is always positive (from + 3.29 +3.29 pp to + 21.03 +21.03 pp) but not always individually significant, since each slice is small; we read them as evidence of a consistent direction rather than of significance in every subgroup. Bucket boundaries were fixed in advance rather than searched. Intuitively, an early mistake costs little context, so a second attempt is cheap and effective; a late mistake sits on top of a long history, and what the agent most needs is not another chance to reason but the one action that gets it back on track. The hard SFT only checks whether the predicted correct/incorrect token matches the label, so it cannot order two actions that receive the same token. We therefore also compare the log-probability each action assigns to that token (Soft). Even so, SFT still under-performs BT, which suggests that SFT learns absolute correctness well, while relative preference is better learned through the pairwise BT loss. Scale also matters. Scaling the data from 128K to 256K adds 1.1 points on UI-Genie and 3 points on AndroidFlux on UI-Genie RM BT, so AndroidFlux still separates reward models where UI-Genie is close to saturation. Still, both reward models stay near chance on AndroidFlux. This indicates that UI-Genie’s preference data, built by injecting errors into clean trajectories, does not provide enough signal to learn recovery. The GUI experts, in contrast, already hold these preferences. Without any reward-model training, their likelihoods reach 0.71 0.71 – 0.74 0.74 on UI-Genie and 0.58 0.58 – 0.60 0.60 on AndroidFlux. Training on the UI-Genie reward modeling dataset alone provides little overall benefit and reduces recovery from first-error states. Training exclusively at the first-error checkpoint produces the strongest recovery but degrades clean-start performance, indicating that concentrating only on failure states can over-specialize the policy. These results suggest that our offline RL dataset provides a more persistent learning signal in both clean runs and failure recovery. Despite the performance differences on both the UI-Genie and AndroidFlux reward modeling evaluation sets, Figure 4 indicates that optimization remains stable across all data mixtures. The mean GPRS reward rises similarly in every run, but it is not a direct measure of policy quality, since the statistic is inflated by duplicate sampled actions within each group. Indeed, the UI-Genie 100% run reaches a comparable final GPRS reward despite the weakest downstream performance. The underlying reward-model scores show a clearer difference: UI-Genie-only training plateaus and then declines later in training, whereas most runs with diverse contexts around the error step keep improving through the final training window, ending with a larger net gain. Overall, these results indicate that our policy-induced failure contexts provide an informative training signal in offline RL for generalized GUI agents without computationally heavy online environments. 6 Limitations and Conclusion We introduced AndroidFlux, a benchmark that evaluates mobile-use agents on recovering from policy-induced first errors and reward models on ranking recovery actions. However, it covers only AndroidWorld and first recoverable errors that can be reconstructed by replay or snapshots, so chains of interacting errors and other GUI environments remain open. The LLM-verified set also inherits noise and source-model imbalance from the detector–verifier pipeline, and recovery success remains sensitive to Android nondeterminism. Even so, our results show that recovering from a committed error is a capability distinct from clean-start success, with domain-specific RL and agentic frameworks far more robust than general-purpose or imitation-trained models. Our reward modeling benchmark demonstrates that reward models trained on conventional GUI preferences stay near chance on recovery states, while the likelihoods of GUI expert agents rank recovery actions more accurately. Furthermore, we find that our curated offline RL dataset improves both clean-start and recovery success under a fixed training budget, showing that policy-induced failure states are effective training signal. Together, our contributions and findings establish failure recovery and recovery-aware reward modeling as key evaluation targets for building robust GUI agents. For the 65 replay-based cases, we re-execute in the emulator the source model’s recorded action sequence through the annotated first-error step t t . A case is considered replayable when this procedure reaches the same erroneous state observed in the original trajectory. Once that state is reached, the recovering policy takes over and continues the task from the restored state. Its inherited history is constructed from the source trajectory metadata and rendered in the target policy’s native format, as detailed in Appendix C.8 . For the remaining 15 cases, replaying the recorded actions from the task’s initial state does not reproduce the original error state. A primary source of such mismatch is residual environment state from preceding tasks. For example, when the original AndroidWorld tasks are executed sequentially, previously used applications may change their positions in recency-ordered interfaces; replaying an individual task in isolation does not reproduce this preceding interaction history and can therefore lead to a different state despite executing the same actions. For these cases, we manually reconstruct the emulator to match the original error state and save it as a VM snapshot, allowing evaluation to resume directly from that state. The inherited history remains based on the original source trajectory, with only the minimal state-dependent details responsible for the replay mismatch adjusted to remain consistent with the reconstructed state. The recovering policy then receives this reconstructed state and history under the same evaluation protocol as in the replay-based cases. Each step is viewed as a triple of (intended goal direction, chosen action, observed screen transition), and the three classes are distinguished by which element of this triple is broken. Classes are checked in a fixed priority order — stagnation → \rightarrow direction → \rightarrow execution — so that a repeated action is labeled as stagnation without further inspecting its direction or realization. Figure 5 shows, for each class, the screen immediately before and after a representative first-error step (a: stagnation, b: direction, c: execution), and Tables 21 and 22 summarize the per-category counts for the two verified sets. Stagnation. The agent re-issues an action that has already failed on an essentially unchanged screen, or oscillates between states, so that the trajectory makes no visible progress (Fig. 5(a) ). The failure lies not in what the agent intends but in the fact that it repeats the attempt without adapting. A first unsuccessful attempt is not counted: the error step is the point at which repetition is established (typically the second or later identical attempt), and actions with intrinsically subtle visual effects (e.g., text editing, keyboard input) are excluded from the “no screen change” criterion. Observed sub-patterns include identical re-taps on the same element, repeated scrolling over an unchanged list, re-entering an already-failed route, and acting on a nonexistent or already-achieved UI state. Direction. The action executes successfully, but it moves the trajectory away from the goal (Fig. 5(b) ): the agent commits to a visibly wrong target, screen, date, or app, regresses by dismissing progress it has already achieved, abandons a route on which the required affordance is already exposed, or ignores a visible contradiction. Local execution is correct; the choice is not. Exploratory route-opening, reversible entries into a wrong menu, and app switches for source verification are protected as valid — a direction error is assigned only when a wrong target or state is committed, or when the agent leaves a required screen without justification. This class subsumes goal-regressive, goal-irrelevant, goal-direction, and unhandled system-error behaviors in our finer-grained taxonomy. Execution. The agent targets the right element with the right kind of action, but the action’s local effect is wrong or absent (Fig. 5(c) ): the committed text, value, or selection differs from the intent, the tap lands on a neighboring control, or a launch/save/toggle produces no state change. The plan is correct; the realization is not. The judgment unit is strictly the current step’s intent versus its immediate outcome — an error is assigned when the immediately following screenshot shows an incorrect committed value, but not merely because the overall task remains unfinished, and stale UI or a missing toast after a correctly targeted commit is not presumed to be a failure. Boundary between stagnation and execution. “No screen change” appears in both classes; the distinction is repetition. The first task-critical action that produces no effect (e.g., an app launch or toggle that fails) is an execution error, whereas re-attempting an action that has already failed is stagnation. Human-verified labels follow this convention consistently. Distributions across verified sets. Tables 21 and 22 break down the first-error class of every verified trajectory by the source model that produced it: the first row of each table gives the overall class distribution of the set, and the remaining rows show, for each source model, how many of its error trajectories fall into each class. In the human-verified set, direction errors are the largest class overall (43.75%), and all three classes occur for every source model; the balance shifts by model, with direction dominating for GUI-Owl-32B and Qwen3-VL-2B, while MAI-UI-8B and Qwen3-VL-4B fail most often at execution.
